paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn several related networks of statistical relationships while incorporating existing domain knowledge. The setting involves sparse Gaussian graphical models, where relatively few interactions are retained. Applications such as neuroscience can involve many variables and many related tasks, making both the use of prior knowledge and computational scalability important.

The proposed estimator, JEEK, represents domain knowledge through weights. Its optimization objective combines two sparsity constraints: one for interactions shared across tasks and another for patterns specific to individual tasks. This gives the method a common way to incorporate different kinds of knowledge without requiring a separate optimization design for each kind.

JEEK also permits parallel computation for individual matrix entries. The stated computational complexity improves from O(p^5 K^4) to O(p^2 K^4), while the statistical analysis establishes the same convergence rate as harder-to-compute estimators. Experiments on synthetic data and neuroscience data report substantially faster computation with comparable prediction accuracy, supporting the value of the computational simplification.
icml-2018-a-fast-and-scalable-joint-esti.tldr: JEEK incorporates domain knowledge into related sparse graphical models while substantially reducing computation and retaining established statistical convergence rates.

paragraphs: The paper considers sequential decisions where the cost of trying an inferior option changes with environmental conditions. Testing a network configuration, for example, can be less costly when network load is low. This creates an opportunity to schedule exploration around the consequences of mistakes, rather than treating every decision as equally expensive.

The authors introduce opportunistic bandits and an algorithm called Adaptive Upper-Confidence-Bound, or AdaUCB. Its guiding principle is to explore more when mistakes cost little and rely more on the best-known option when mistakes are expensive. Environmental variation therefore becomes useful information for deciding when to learn and when to exploit existing knowledge.

The analysis establishes logarithmic regret with a smaller coefficient than traditional UCB. A stronger, constant-regret result applies if exploration has zero cost below a particular load threshold; it is conditional on that special setting. Experiments using synthetic data and real-world traces report substantial gains over UCB and Thompson Sampling when load or price fluctuates strongly.
icml-2018-adaptive-exploration-exploitat.tldr: AdaUCB uses changing environmental costs to explore when mistakes are cheaper, improving regret guarantees and empirical performance in opportunistic bandits.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty through a distribution over model parameters. Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics can learn this distribution by generating parameter samples from small batches of training data. Keeping many such samples, however, means storing many versions of the network, which can become prohibitively expensive for large models.

Adversarial Posterior Distillation addresses this storage problem by training a generative adversarial network on the parameter samples. At prediction time, the generator produces samples instead of relying on a stored collection of network copies. The object being distilled is the parameter posterior itself, extending beyond a summary of the network's predictive outputs.

That distinction matters because posterior samples support calculations such as approximate model variance, which can be useful in subsequent tasks. The authors report no performance loss from distillation in the applications they examine: anomaly detection, active learning, and defense against adversarial attacks. These findings support the approach as a practical way to retain useful Bayesian uncertainty information while changing how posterior samples are represented.
icml-2018-adversarial-distillation-of-ba.tldr: Adversarial Posterior Distillation trains a GAN to generate Bayesian network parameter samples, retaining useful uncertainty information without storing every sampled network.

paragraphs: Choosing a regularization parameter determines how strongly a regression model is constrained during fitting. This tuning problem becomes computationally challenging when both the number of observations and the number of parameters are large. The paper targets leave-one-out cross-validation risk, using an efficient approximation to support parameter selection in this setting.

The authors develop two approximation frameworks, one based on the primal formulation of penalized regression and the other on its dual formulation. Both address models with nonsmooth losses or regularizers. Under smoothness conditions, they prove that the two approaches are equivalent and use this connection to justify the accuracy of their approximations.

The frameworks yield risk estimates for generalized LASSO, nuclear norm regularization, and support vector machines. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in nondifferentiable cases, extending the practical evidence beyond the smooth setting covered by the stated equivalence argument. The contribution is therefore both a pair of computational approaches and an explanation of how they relate under specific mathematical conditions.
icml-2018-approximate-leave-one-out-for-.tldr: Two primal and dual frameworks efficiently approximate leave-one-out risk for tuning penalized regression, including models with nonsmooth components.

paragraphs: Numerical integration uses finite information to approximate a continuous mathematical quantity. Bayesian quadrature represents the resulting uncertainty with a posterior distribution over the integral. This paper asks whether that probabilistic treatment can do more than express uncertainty when several related functions need to be integrated.

The proposed method extends Bayesian quadrature so that information can be transferred between related integration problems. Instead of treating each computation as isolated, it uses their relationships within a shared probabilistic approach. The authors argue that this can produce a more faithful representation of uncertainty and, as an additional benefit, improve numerical efficiency.

The paper establishes convergence rates for both well-specified and misspecified cases, addressing settings where the modeling assumptions fit the problem and settings where they do not. Applications to engineering models with different fidelity levels and to global illumination in computer graphics demonstrate efficiency. The central contribution is to make relationships between numerical problems useful within the computation itself, alongside the uncertainty estimates that Bayesian numerical methods already provide.
icml-2018-bayesian-quadrature-for-multip.tldr: An extension of Bayesian quadrature shares information across related integrals to improve uncertainty representation and numerical efficiency.

paragraphs: Distributed matrix multiplication can be delayed by a few slow or faulty processors, often called stragglers. Coded computation introduces redundancy so that the final result can be recovered despite delayed work. For sparse matrices, however, existing coding schemes can undermine the computational benefits of having many zero entries.

The paper introduces a strategy called sparse code for computing a matrix product of the form A-transpose times B. It aims to combine resilience to stragglers with low computation overhead. A central result is a near-optimal recovery threshold, meaning that the amount of completed distributed work needed for recovery is close to optimal.

The method also decodes in time linear in the number of nonzero entries of the output matrix, O(nnz(C)), rather than scaling with all r times t output positions. This distinction is especially relevant when the output is sparse. An implementation demonstrates advantages over both uncoded computation and the fastest existing coded strategies considered by the authors, connecting the theoretical design to measured computational benefits.
icml-2018-coded-sparse-matrix-multiplica.tldr: Sparse code makes distributed matrix multiplication resilient to stragglers while achieving near-optimal recovery and decoding time proportional to output nonzeros.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning attempts to infer a reward function from observed behavior. This paper studies that problem in zero-sum stochastic games, where agents compete and the demonstrations are known to be imperfect. Assuming that demonstrators already behave optimally would remove an important part of the problem the authors want to address.

Their objective directly compares expert behavior against Nash equilibrium policies, keeping the competitive relationship between agents in the learning problem. They develop an algorithm for recovering rewards using deep neural networks as approximations. To obtain equilibrium policies in large games, they also introduce an adversarial training procedure for zero-sum stochastic games.

The authors identify a theoretical property of the equilibrium objective: the absence of local optima. Their numerical experiments show that the equilibrium and reward-learning algorithms handle games that existing benchmark algorithms cannot address. They also report successful recovery of rewards and policies across the demonstration qualities examined. These experimental findings support learning from imperfect competitors without treating demonstration optimality as a prerequisite.
icml-2018-competitive-multi-agent-invers.tldr: The paper learns rewards in competitive zero-sum games by comparing imperfect demonstrations with Nash equilibrium policies.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning changes which training examples a model encounters as learning proceeds. This paper first examines an ideal curriculum mathematically for stochastic gradient descent on a convex linear regression loss. That setting provides a tractable way to study how example difficulty and the model's current errors relate to convergence.

The analysis proves that the convergence rate of the ideal method increases monotonically with example difficulty. Among examples of equal difficulty, those producing greater loss under the current hypothesis lead to faster convergence. The authors then construct a practical curriculum for a convolutional network using information transferred from another network pretrained on a different task.

This transferred curriculum only approximates the ideal one, so the neural-network findings are empirical. The experiments nevertheless show a substantial acceleration early in training, resembling the behavior predicted by the theory. Generalization also improves when the task is made harder, and curriculum learning shows robustness to unfavorable conditions such as excessive regularization. These results connect a restricted theoretical analysis with a practical curriculum-building method.
icml-2018-curriculum-learning-by-transfe.tldr: The paper analyzes ideal curricula for linear regression and uses transfer learning to build practical curricula that accelerate early CNN training.

paragraphs: Convolutional layers can account for much of a neural network's computation and parameter storage, creating pressure to reduce both model size and energy use. This paper targets those layers through weight sharing. It clusters convolutional weights so that many weights can be represented by the same learned value.

The compressed representation stores K cluster centers together with indexes indicating which center each weight uses. During retraining, a new spectrally relaxed k-means regularizer encourages weights toward harder assignments to these centers. This makes the training procedure support the shared-weight representation that will ultimately provide compression.

The authors also propose metrics for estimating energy consumption in CNN hardware implementations. Their estimates agree with an existing estimation tool derived from hardware measurements, providing support for that evaluation approach. Across several CNN models, they report promising compression and estimated energy reductions without accuracy loss in the evaluated cases. The work therefore links a concrete parameter-sharing scheme with retraining and an assessment of its potential hardware energy benefits.
icml-2018-deep-k-means-re-training-and-p.tldr: Deep k-Means compresses convolutional weights through clustering and retraining, with reported compression and energy benefits without accuracy loss.

paragraphs: This paper builds an image-recognition network around predictive coding, a neuroscience theory in which representations are refined through predictions and their errors. The resulting deep predictive coding network includes feedforward, feedback, and recurrent connections. Its recognition process involves repeated computation over an image rather than a single pass through the layers.

Higher layers send predictions of lower-layer representations through feedback connections. Lower layers send prediction errors upward through feedforward connections. Repeated bottom-up and top-down cycles update the internal representations to reduce discrepancies between incoming information and predictions. After several cycles, the network uses the refined representation to classify the image.

On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and MNIST, the authors report that the predictive coding network consistently outperformed its feedforward-only counterpart. Performance also tended to improve when more computation cycles were allowed. The findings support recurrent refinement as a useful component of the tested recognition architecture, while the reported tendency with additional cycles does not imply that every extra cycle necessarily improves every prediction.
icml-2018-deep-predictive-coding-network.tldr: A predictive coding network repeatedly exchanges predictions and errors between layers, improving object recognition over its feedforward-only counterpart in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programming languages let users describe uncertain models and then perform inference about them. The paper addresses a gap in their support for variables whose distributions contain both discrete and continuous elements. Handling these mixtures requires a mathematical foundation broad enough to describe both parts within the same probabilistic model.

The authors introduce measure-theoretic Bayesian networks, or MTBNs, to supply that foundation. Their framework supports arbitrarily many random variables defined over arbitrary measure spaces. They use it to give probabilistic programs more general semantics: a precise account of what the programs mean as probabilistic objects.

The paper also develops two sampling algorithms with correctness guarantees under this framework. Lexicographic likelihood weighting applies to general MTBNs, while the lexicographic particle filter specializes to state-space models. The authors integrate the framework into BLOG and demonstrate the inference algorithms on representative examples. The contribution thus joins broader modeling semantics with concrete inference procedures and an implementation in an existing probabilistic programming system.
icml-2018-discrete-continuous-mixtures-i.tldr: Measure-theoretic Bayesian networks extend probabilistic programming to mixed discrete-continuous distributions and support two provably correct sampling algorithms.

paragraphs: In distributed learning, several machines compute gradients from different portions of the data. Exchanging those gradients can become a bottleneck, even when the machines can perform their local calculations quickly. This paper focuses on reducing the communication needed for stochastic gradient descent while maintaining effective optimization.

The proposed method quantizes local gradients, representing them more compactly before communication. Quantization introduces discrepancies between the original gradients and the transmitted versions. The algorithm retains accumulated quantization error and uses it to improve subsequent optimization, making the error information part of the learning procedure rather than simply losing it.

The authors analyze convergence and present advantages over competing approaches. Their experiments indicate gradient compression of up to two orders of magnitude without performance degradation in the evaluated settings. This result connects communication savings with preserved learning performance, rather than considering compression alone. The paper's central contribution is the combination of compact gradient messages and explicit compensation for the information those messages leave out.
icml-2018-error-compensated-quantized-sg.tldr: Error-compensated quantized SGD reduces gradient communication and reuses accumulated quantization error, achieving substantial experimental compression without performance degradation.

paragraphs: A trained recurrent neural network carries information through a changing internal state. This paper asks how to extract a deterministic finite automaton that describes those state dynamics. The desired output is a discrete description of the trained network's behavior, giving the extraction procedure a specific object to construct and assess.

The method combines exact learning with abstraction. Angluin's L-star algorithm serves as the learner, while the trained recurrent network serves as the oracle that the learner consults. Queries and counterexamples support the extraction process, and abstraction connects the network's state representation with the finite-state description being learned. These components place learning and state representation within a single algorithm.

The authors report that the technique efficiently extracts accurate automata even when the recurrent network has large state vectors that require fine distinctions. This matters because an extraction method must preserve behaviorally relevant differences while producing a discrete model. The stated result concerns accurate descriptions of trained networks, including cases where their internal representations are large and cannot be treated coarsely.
icml-2018-extracting-automata-from-recur.tldr: The paper combines exact learning and abstraction to efficiently extract accurate finite automata describing trained RNN state dynamics.

paragraphs: A general-purpose solver can behave very differently under different configurations. This paper studies how to choose a configuration that runs quickly on average over most instances from an unknown distribution. The search itself consumes computation, so the objective includes limiting the total work spent testing candidate configurations.

LeapsAndBounds evaluates configurations on randomly selected instances, allowing progressively longer execution times. Each trial can end when the solver finishes or reaches a timeout. This setup lets the configurator gather runtime evidence while controlling how much work individual tests consume as the search proceeds.

The authors prove that the returned configuration has capped expected runtime close to the optimal expected runtime, and that the configurator's own runtime is near-optimal. The cap is part of the stated performance guarantee and should remain part of its interpretation. They also establish greater efficiency than the earlier theoretically guaranteed method they compare against. Experiments configuring a public SAT solver on a new benchmark dataset support the method's practical advantages.
icml-2018-leapsandbounds-a-method-for-ap.tldr: LeapsAndBounds progressively extends solver trials to find configurations with near-optimal capped expected runtime while using near-optimal search effort.

paragraphs: The paper studies a local counting problem for high-dimensional vector data: given a query vector and a distance threshold, estimate how many stored vectors fall within that distance. Such a count describes how densely populated the query's neighborhood is. The goal is to answer these queries accurately and efficiently.

The algorithm preprocesses the vectors with locality sensitive hashing and constructs an unbiased estimator using importance sampling. Unbiasedness means that the estimator is correct on average over its sampling randomness, rather than that every individual estimate equals the true count. The sampling procedure provides the statistical basis for estimating the neighborhood population.

A central design feature is sampling from multiple buckets within each hash table. Supporting data structures and preprocessing allow the method to operate with a small number of tables. The authors provide bounds on storage requirements and query complexity, linking this design to computational costs. Experiments on a standard word-embedding dataset demonstrate effectiveness for the kind of learned vector representations that motivate the problem.
icml-2018-local-density-estimation-in-hi.tldr: The method combines locality sensitive hashing and importance sampling to estimate neighborhood counts using few hash tables.

paragraphs: The paper studies online decisions informed by many measured variables when only a small subset is relevant. Its MCP-Bandit algorithm uses a minimax concave penalty to exploit this latent sparse structure. The aim is to make effective sequential choices while learning which parts of the high-dimensional information matter.

The authors show that cumulative regret asymptotically grows as O(log T), achieving the stated optimal dependence on the number of decisions. They also derive tighter dependence on the overall covariate dimension and the number of significant covariates. These results connect decision quality to sparsity, rather than treating every available variable as equally consequential.

To compute the required estimator from non-independent, non-identically distributed samples, the paper develops a two-step weighted Lasso approximation. This procedure matches the oracle estimator with high probability. Two experiments show favorable performance relative to other bandit algorithms, particularly when the data are highly sparse or the sample size is not too small. Those qualifications identify where the reported empirical advantages are especially pronounced.
icml-2018-minimax-concave-penalized-mult.tldr: MCP-Bandit exploits sparse structure in high-dimensional decision data, with asymptotically optimal logarithmic regret and favorable experimental results.

paragraphs: Convolutional sparse coding learns filters that can capture patterns at different positions in images or signals. Existing methods can have difficulty scaling to large datasets. This paper changes the dictionary representation so that the collection of filters can adapt to each sample rather than being identical across all samples.

Each sample-dependent filter is a linear combination of a small collection of base filters learned from data. This construction combines a compact shared foundation with flexibility in the patterns available for individual samples. The authors argue that the resulting ability to capture many sample-specific patterns is especially useful for large or high-dimensional datasets.

The model can be learned efficiently through online learning, which is a key part of its computational approach. Across a number of datasets, the authors report that it outperforms existing convolutional sparse coding algorithms while substantially reducing time and space complexity. The findings support the combination of a flexible dictionary representation and an online learning procedure as a way to improve both modeling and scalability.
icml-2018-online-convolutional-sparse-co.tldr: Sample-dependent combinations of shared base filters make convolutional sparse coding more flexible and enable efficient online learning.

paragraphs: This paper trains ReLU classifiers using guarantees about adversarial perturbations whose size is bounded by a norm. It considers the internal activations reachable under those perturbations and encloses them in a convex outer approximation. Optimizing against this larger region provides bounds on the loss that an allowed adversary could cause.

The robust objective minimizes worst-case loss over the outer region through a linear program. The authors show that the corresponding dual problem can itself be represented as a deep network resembling backpropagation. This representation enables efficient optimization using additional forward and backward passes, although substantially larger batches may be needed.

The approach gives robustness guarantees on training data and an unseen-example detection guarantee that permits false alarms on non-adversarial inputs. In the MNIST example, a convolutional classifier has certified test error below 5.8% for attacks with infinity-norm perturbation below 0.1. The result illustrates a guarantee over the specified perturbation set, rather than evidence limited to success against particular attack algorithms.
icml-2018-provable-defenses-against-adve.tldr: A convex relaxation of reachable activations enables efficient robust training and certified guarantees against norm-bounded adversarial perturbations.

paragraphs: High-dimensional datasets often contain many redundant features, making downstream analysis more expensive than necessary. This paper considers a streaming setting where features are revealed sequentially and their importance must be assessed online. The focus is selecting a useful feature space for subsequent k-means clustering while providing a rigorous account of its quality.

The proposed selection algorithm uses online leverage scores to evaluate features as they arrive. The retained features are then supplied to k-means. Working in this selected space makes the clustering stage more efficient in memory and computation, giving feature selection a direct role in reducing the cost of the downstream task.

The authors prove that, with high probability, clustering in the selected feature space stays close to the optimal clustering available from the original data. This is a probabilistic approximation guarantee, not a claim that the two clusterings must always coincide. Experiments on real-world datasets support the method's effectiveness, complementing the theoretical link between online feature selection and clustering quality.
icml-2018-provable-variable-selection-fo.tldr: Online leverage scores select streaming features for efficient k-means clustering with a high-probability approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether confidence information already present in an adversarially trained model can help strengthen its robustness. It measures confidence using the largest component of the model's output. The key question is whether that value can help distinguish correct predictions from incorrect ones near a typical data point.

The authors analyze an existing adversarial training objective and show that, under a variety of instantiations, even a moderately good solution can make confidence informative in this local sense. The result links the training objective to a useful property of the resulting confidence scores. It does not assert that arbitrary models have universally reliable confidence.

Based on that analysis, the paper proposes Highly Confident Near Neighbor, a framework combining confidence information with nearest-neighbor search to reinforce a base model. The authors develop algorithms within the framework and conduct a detailed empirical study. They describe the results as encouraging and supportive of their analysis, while also reporting problems observed with existing adversarial training. The contribution centers on making locally informative confidence useful for robustness.
icml-2018-reinforcing-adversarial-robust.tldr: Highly Confident Near Neighbor combines confidence induced by adversarial training with neighbor search to strengthen a base model's robustness.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems need rankings tailored to individual users while drawing information from many users together. This paper models whole ranked lists, rather than treating each rating or each pairwise comparison as an independent example. The listwise formulation makes the ordering itself the central object of collaborative learning.

The authors assign probabilities to permutations using a low-rank matrix of latent user-item scores and learn through maximum likelihood. Their SQL-Rank algorithm accommodates tied preferences and missing observations and can run in linear time. These properties make the proposed ranking model applicable when the available preference information is incomplete or does not define a strict ordering.

The paper also develops a representation-based theoretical framework for permutation models and derives asymptotic statistical rates as user and item counts grow together. Empirically, SQL-Rank often outperforms Weighted-MF and BPR on implicit feedback and compares favorably with methods for explicit feedback. The wording matters: these are favorable comparative findings, not a claim of dominance on every recommendation problem.
icml-2018-sql-rank-a-listwise-approach-t.tldr: SQL-Rank learns collaborative user rankings through a listwise permutation model that supports ties, missing data, and linear-time computation.

paragraphs: Inference in a continuous graphical model must account for dependencies among variables, potentially in a high-dimensional distribution. This paper extends Stein variational gradient descent so that its computations explicitly use the model's Markov structure. The aim is to reduce difficulties associated with high dimensionality while enabling distributed inference.

The method uses structured local kernel functions defined over each node's Markov blanket, the local collection of variables relevant to its conditional relationships. These local kernels organize the inference procedure around the dependency structure. The resulting algorithm can distribute its computations, making the same design useful for decentralized inference tasks.

The theoretical analysis interprets the method as a localized approximation that matches the target's nodewise conditional distributions over their Markov blankets. This describes the particular probabilistic relationships the approximation preserves. Experiments report improvements over several baselines, including standard MCMC and particle message passing. Together, the analysis and empirical findings support using graphical structure to shape the approximation rather than treating the distribution as an undifferentiated high-dimensional object.
icml-2018-stein-variational-message-pass.tldr: Local Markov-blanket kernels extend Stein variational inference into a distributed method that alleviates high-dimensional inference difficulties.

paragraphs: Speech synthesis must represent how words are spoken as well as which words are spoken. This paper introduces global style tokens, a bank of learned embeddings trained jointly with Tacotron. The training uses no explicit style labels, yet the embeddings capture a broad range of acoustic expressiveness.

The learned tokens provide soft, interpretable labels that can control aspects of synthesis such as speed and speaking style independently of text content. They also support style transfer: a single reference audio clip can supply a speaking style that is reproduced across a long collection of text. This connects unsupervised style learning with direct control over generated speech.

When trained on noisy, unlabeled found data, the system learns to separate noise and speaker identity into factors. The authors present this as a possible route toward scalable and robust speech synthesis. That implication is prospective, while the reported style control, transfer, and factorization are the concrete findings supporting it. The work makes unlabeled acoustic variation useful within an end-to-end synthesis system.
icml-2018-style-tokens-unsupervised-styl.tldr: Global style tokens learn expressive speech variation without style labels, enabling control and transfer of speaking style in Tacotron.

paragraphs: Certifying robustness asks how much an input must change before an adversarial example becomes possible. Exact verification for general ReLU networks is computationally hard. This paper instead computes certified lower bounds on the smallest adversarial distortion, providing a guaranteed threshold even when the exact minimum is impractical to obtain.

The authors introduce Fast-Lin and Fast-Lip, which exploit ReLU network structure. On small networks, their bounds are within a factor of two to three of exact minimum distortions computed by Reluplex, with more than a 10,000-fold speed advantage. On larger networks, they report bounds of similar quality to linear-programming methods and substantial speed improvements.

The experiments also cover MNIST and CIFAR networks with up to seven layers and more than 10,000 neurons, processed within tens of seconds on one CPU core. Separately, the paper proves a conditional hardness result: unless P equals NP, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves the stated 0.99 ln n approximation ratio for minimum l1 adversarial distortion. This distinguishes fast certification of lower bounds from solving the underlying minimum-distortion problem.
icml-2018-towards-fast-computation-of-ce.tldr: Fast-Lin and Fast-Lip efficiently certify lower bounds on adversarial distortion by exploiting ReLU network structure.

paragraphs: Off-policy learning improves a decision policy using historical data gathered by a different logging policy. This is useful when evaluating new decisions directly is expensive or has adverse consequences. A central challenge is controlling the variance of counterfactual estimates so that conclusions from logged data generalize reliably.

The paper introduces a learning principle for bandit feedback inspired by bounds for importance sampling. It regularizes generalization error by minimizing a distribution divergence between the logging policy and the new policy. This makes the relationship between the two policies part of the optimization objective, linking policy learning to the statistical stability of its estimates.

The approach avoids the need to pass through all training samples to compute the sample-variance regularization used in earlier work. For neural-network policies, the authors develop end-to-end training algorithms based on variational divergence minimization. Their experiments show significant improvements over conventional baselines, consistent with the theoretical results. The contribution combines an alternative way to control generalization with a training procedure that removes a particular computational burden of variance regularization.
icml-2018-variance-regularized-counterfa.tldr: Divergence-based regularization supports off-policy neural policy learning while avoiding full-data sample-variance calculations used by earlier methods.
